lines.text: A Lewis structure is a diagram that shows how a molecule's valence electrons are arranged. We draw shared bonding pairs as lines, and unshared lone pairs as dots. The arrangement is guided by the octet rule, where main group atoms tend to form bonds until they are surrounded by eight valence electrons.

Let's build H C N. First, count the valence electrons: one plus four plus five equals ten. Second, draw a skeleton with single bonds. H is never central, so carbon is in the middle. This uses four electrons. Third, complete terminal octets. H only gets two, so we put the remaining six electrons on nitrogen. Finally, carbon lacks an octet, so we convert two of nitrogen's lone pairs into bonding pairs, creating a triple bond.

When multiple structures are possible, we use formal charge to choose the best one. Formal charge is the valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons. For C O two, a structure with two double bonds gives all atoms a formal charge of zero. A structure with a triple and single bond gives the oxygens charges of plus one and minus one. The structure with all zero formal charges is preferred.

Sometimes, two or more valid structures can be drawn. For O three, we can draw a double bond on the left or the right. These are resonance structures. The real molecule is not a mixture that flips between them. It is a single resonance hybrid, an average of both structures. Both bonds in O three are equal at one hundred twenty-eight picometers, between a single and a double bond.

Remember these common pitfalls. The octet rule has exceptions. Hydrogen is full with two electrons. B F three is electron deficient, N O has an odd number, and S F six has an expanded octet. Also, formal charge is not a real electrical charge; it is just hypothetical bookkeeping that assumes electrons are shared equally.
